rationale: An adversarial evaluation of available clinical and genetic literature indicates that individuals with biallelic FILIP1 variants present with normal or only mildly elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) levels, typically within normal limits or up to mild elevations resembling female dystrophinopathy carriers rather than severe primary dystrophies. In contrast, classical dystrophinopathies (DMD) and severe congenital muscular dystrophies like LAMA2-related dystrophy routinely manifest marked serum CK elevations (frequently 10x to >50x upper limit of normal). No reports of severe, persistent hyperCKemia (>10x ULN) were identified in FILIP1-related neuromuscular disorder cohorts.

evidence.text: In a phenotypic analysis of FILIP1-associated neuromuscular disorder, creatine kinase levels were found to be mildly elevated (in the range typical of manifesting female DMD carriers rather than classic severe dystrophinopathies), particularly noted in an affected younger sibling.

new_directions.question_text: Does serum creatine kinase fluctuate with age, disease progression, or ambulatory status in FILIP1-related neuromuscular disorder?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying whether mild hyperCKemia in FILIP1-associated disorders diminishes with muscle wasting or is purely static will refine its utility as a differential diagnostic biomarker.

new_directions.question_text: What specific dysmorphic facies and joint contracture patterns best differentiate congenital FILIP1 disorders from other congenital myopathies with normal-to-mild CK elevations?
new_directions.rationale: While CK distinguishes FILIP1 from dystrophinopathies and LAMA2-RD, other congenital myopathies (e.g., RYR1, NEB) also feature normal-to-mild CK; distinctive craniofacial and arthrogrypotic phenotypes are critical for clinical differentiation.
